claims.text: On the afternoon of January 15, 1919, a giant tank released 2,300,000 gallons of molasses over Commercial Street in Boston's North End.
claims.quote: A 50-foot wave of molasses—2,300,000 gallons of it—released in some manner yet unexplained, from a giant tank, swept over Commercial street and its waterfront from Charter street to the southerly end of North End Park yesterday afternoon.

claims.text: The wave swept Commercial Street and its waterfront from Charter Street to the southern end of North End Park.
claims.quote: swept over Commercial street and its waterfront from Charter street to the southerly end of North End Park yesterday afternoon

claims.text: The flood caught more than 100 men, women and children, and crushed buildings, horse teams, automobiles and street cars.
claims.quote: Ensnaring in its sticky flood more than 100 men, women and children, crushing buildings, teams, automobiles and street cars—everything in its path

claims.text: The mass struck the buildings facing Copp's Hill and then swept back towards the harbour.
claims.quote: the black, reeking mass slapped against the side of the buildings fronting Copp's Hill and then swished back towards the harbor

claims.text: By midnight the next day's paper counted eleven known dead, a woman, a girl and nine men, and more than 50 injured.
claims.quote: Eleven persons—a woman, a girl and nine men—were the known dead at midnight. More than 50 injured were in hospitals and at their homes.

claims.text: The final toll was 21 dead and about 150 injured.
claims.notes: S6 (supplied excerpt, paraphrase; tier 2) supports it; other sources still unread leads. One secondary source for a number: a second independent one is needed

claims.text: How high the wave was is disputed: the Boston Post reported 50 feet; later accounts give figures from about 15 to 40 feet, most often 25 feet.
claims.quote: Giant Wave of 2,300,000 Gallons of Molasses, 50 Feet High
claims.notes: The 50-foot figure equals the tank's reported height; modern figures UNVERIFIED (search summaries)

claims.text: The wave is estimated to have moved at about 35 miles an hour.
claims.notes: S6 (supplied excerpt, paraphrase; tier 2) supports it; also in the Commons description (S11). A modern estimate, not a measurement: say 'about'

claims.text: The elevated railway structure on Commercial Street was crushed.
claims.quote: Buildings, Vehicles and L Structure Crushed

claims.text: Among the dead was George Lahey (as the Post spells it), an engineer of Engine 31 of the Boston Fire Department.
claims.quote: ENGINEER GEORGE LAHEY, Engine 31, B. F. D., 401 Saratoga street, East Boston

claims.text: Among the unidentified dead was a girl of about 14 with an employment tag from the Revere Rubber Company.
claims.quote: Girl about 14 years of age. She wore a gray jacket over a woolen middy blouse and carried a bag with an employment tag of the Revere Rubber Company.

claims.text: Dead horses, cats and dogs were carted away, and Boston's only trolley freight terminal was in ruins.
claims.quote: Dead horses, cats and dogs had been carted away in team after team. Boston's only trolley freight terminal was in ruins.

claims.text: Ambulances were rushed from all over the city, and rescuers worked on the North End Park playground.
claims.quote: Ambulances from all sections of the city were rushed to the scene

claims.text: The day after, a state police chemist, W. L. Wedger, concluded that an internal explosion, not a collapse, had caused the disaster; this first explanation did not stand.
claims.quote: W. L. Wedger, State police chemist in charge of explosives, had reached the positive conclusion that the disaster instead of being due to a collapse of the great tank was caused by an internal explosion
claims.notes: Contemporary theory only. Against it: S6 (supplied excerpt) gives structural causes (C27, C28) and a 1925 finding of negligence (C29). The script must present the explosion theory as an early, later rejected explanation

claims.text: On January 15, 1919, 35 states had ratified the Prohibition amendment and one more was needed.
claims.quote: Amendment Ratified by Five Yesterday—One More Needed—Predict Nation Dry July 1

claims.text: The tank belonged to the Purity Distilling Company, a subsidiary of United States Industrial Alcohol.
claims.notes: UNVERIFIED: from web-search summaries only; confirm before publishing. S6 supports Purity Distilling as the builder (see C25), not the USIA link

claims.text: The tank, about 50 feet tall, was built in 1915, was never properly tested with water, leaked from the start and was painted brown to hide the leaks.
claims.notes: UNVERIFIED: from web-search summaries only; confirm before publishing; sources differ on the build date (1915 or 1917) and the test. S6 supports the 1915 date, the 50 ft height and earlier leaks (C25, C26), not the water test or the brown paint, which stay leads

claims.text: Arthur Jell, the company official who oversaw the tank's construction, had no engineering training.
claims.notes: UNVERIFIED: from web-search summaries only; confirm before publishing

claims.text: After a freezing spell, the temperature rose above 40 degrees Fahrenheit on the day of the disaster.
claims.notes: UNVERIFIED: from web-search summaries only; confirm before publishing. S6 names 'temperature changes' as a factor (C28) but gives no figure; the 40 F figure stays a lead. S6 removed on 2026-11-21: a search summary had linked it to this claim, but the excerpt the producer supplied does not state it

claims.text: A 2016 Harvard study found that the molasses thickened as it cooled in the January air, which trapped victims and hampered rescue.
claims.notes: UNVERIFIED: from web-search summaries only; confirm before publishing

claims.text: A court-appointed auditor, Hugh Ogden, ruled in 1925 that the company was liable, rejecting its claim that anarchists had blown up the tank.
claims.notes: UNVERIFIED: from web-search summaries only; confirm before publishing

claims.text: Reported figures for the damages paid differ: about $628,000 in some accounts, larger settlement totals in others.
claims.notes: UNVERIFIED: from web-search summaries only; confirm before publishing; the figure is disputed among the summaries

claims.text: The cleanup of the immediate area took weeks, and the harbour stayed brown with molasses until summer.
claims.notes: UNVERIFIED: from web-search summaries only; confirm before publishing

claims.text: The disaster led to stricter rules for engineers and construction.
claims.notes: UNVERIFIED: from web-search summaries only; confirm before publishing. S6 removed on 2026-11-21: a search summary had linked it to this claim, but the excerpt the producer supplied does not state it

claims.text: The tank, 50 feet tall and holding about 2.3 million gallons, was built in 1915 by the Purity Distilling Company.
claims.notes: S6 (supplied excerpt, paraphrase; tier 2) supports it; no verbatim quote available

claims.text: The tank had reportedly leaked before the disaster.
claims.notes: S6 (supplied excerpt, paraphrase; tier 2) supports it; no verbatim quote available

claims.text: Structural engineers later found the tank's walls too thin and its material vulnerable to cracking.
claims.notes: S6 (supplied excerpt, paraphrase; tier 2) supports it; no verbatim quote available

claims.text: Poor construction, changes in temperature and a large shipment of molasses together contributed to the rupture.
claims.notes: S6 (supplied excerpt, paraphrase; tier 2) supports it; no verbatim quote available

claims.text: In 1925 a court-appointed auditor attributed the disaster to negligence by the tank's owners.
claims.notes: S6 (supplied excerpt, paraphrase; tier 2) supports it; no verbatim quote available
